lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5, what were Rome's Twelve Tables? (Laws written down for everyone to see.) Today: how England's barons wrote down limits on their own king.
King John ruled England from 1199. He lost lands in France, raised taxes again and again, and punished people without fair trials. By 1215 many barons had turned against him.
On 15 June 1215, at Runnymede beside the River Thames, John agreed to the barons' charter. It was later called Magna Carta, the Great Charter, and it set out rules that the king had to follow too.

Its best-known promise is clause 39: no free man may be jailed or lose his land except by the law. That means the lawful judgement of his equals, or the law of the land. Clause 40: justice will not be sold, refused or delayed.

At first it helped few people: most were peasants who were not free. Within weeks the Pope cancelled it, and war broke out again. But it was issued again in 1216, 1217 and 1225, and became part of England's law.

Kings needed money, so they called meetings of barons and bishops, parliaments, from the French parler, to talk. In 1265 Simon de Montfort also called two knights from each county and two townspeople from each big town: the first time towns were asked.

In 1295 King Edward I called a parliament the same way. In the 1300s it split into two houses: the Lords (barons and bishops) and the Commons (knights and townspeople). Magna Carta's ideas later inspired laws in many countries.

Try it in the world: write a charter for your village or server: rules the leader must follow too, and a fair way to settle arguments. Ask friends to agree to it. Next: the inventions of Tang and Song China.

exercises.prompt: Which king agreed to Magna Carta in 1215?
exercises.explain: King John, at Runnymede on 15 June 1215.

exercises.prompt: Magna Carta said the king had to follow rules too.
exercises.hint: What were the barons trying to stop?
exercises.explain: True: it put limits on the king's power.
Magna Carta is Latin for the Great Charter.

exercises.hint: It was a meadow beside a river west of London.
exercises.explain: At Runnymede, beside the River Thames.

exercises.prompt: Where does the word parliament come from?
exercises.hint: What do people do in a parliament?
exercises.explain: From the French parler, to talk.

exercises.prompt: Magna Carta was agreed in 1215 and issued again in 1225. How many years later was that?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.
It is about being judged fairly.
choices: no free man jailed without a lawful judgement
exercises.explain: No free man could be jailed or lose his land without a lawful judgement.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
exercises.hint: Look at the years: the smaller the year, the earlier.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: who sat in the House of Lords, and who in the Commons, in the 1300s?
exercises.hint: The Lords were the great landowners and churchmen.
exercises.explain: Lords: barons and bishops. Commons: knights from the counties and townspeople.

exercises.prompt: In 1215, Magna Carta helped every person in England equally.
exercises.explain: False: most people were peasants who were not free, so at first it helped barons and free men most.

exercises.prompt: In which year was the 800th anniversary of Magna Carta?
Why did Simon de Montfort's parliament of 1265 matter?
exercises.hint: Who came in 1265 who had never come before?
choices: townspeople were called for the first time
exercises.explain: For the first time, two townspeople from each big town were called, as well as knights from each county.

exercises.prompt: Why did kings keep calling parliaments?
exercises.hint: What did kings always need for their wars and castles?
choices: they needed agreement to raise taxes
exercises.explain: They needed money, and it was easier to raise taxes when parliament agreed.

exercises.prompt: The Pope cancelled Magna Carta in 1215, so it was soon forgotten for ever.
exercises.explain: False: it was issued again in 1216, 1217 and 1225 and became part of the law.

exercises.prompt: Which idea from Magna Carta still matters today?
exercises.hint: What did the barons want the king to follow?
choices: even rulers must obey the law
exercises.explain: Even rulers must obey the law, and people must be judged fairly.

exercises.prompt: Match each clause or date to what it stands for.
exercises.hint: Two are promises in Magna Carta; two are parliaments.
exercises.explain: Clause 39: no free man jailed without a lawful judgement. Clause 40: justice will not be sold, refused or delayed. 1265: Simon de Montfort first asked the towns. 1295: Edward I called a parliament the same way.
